## 2. Governing thought Education is exhausted by four faces of one pyramid: objects, methods, warrants and bridges. Its objects divide into five elements of an educational arrangement: aims and curricula, learners, teaching, assessment, and institutions and systems. ## 3. Key line Dimension: **the element of an educational arrangement.** Order: from purpose to system. 1. Aims and curricula 2. Learners 3. Teaching 4. Assessment 5. Institutions and systems ## 4. Face O — Objects ### ED.O.A1 Aims and curricula **SCQA.** Every arrangement serves a stated aim. What should be learned,

in what order? Key line: aims, curriculum content, sequence and progression. - ED.O.A1.1 Aims — the stated purposes of education. The normative argument for them is PL; the statement of an adopted aim is ED (W12). - ED.O.A1.2 Curriculum content — what is taught. The truth of the content stays with its owner (a theorem is MA). - ED.O.A1.3 Sequence and progression — learning progressions and prerequisites. - ED.O.A1.4 National curricula — e.g. Te Whāriki (NZ early childhood) and Te Marautanga o Aotearoa (Māori-medium) as stated frameworks (W12). ### ED.O.A2

Learners **SCQA.** Learning happens in a learner with prior knowledge. What does the learner bring, and how do they change? Key line: prior knowledge and misconceptions, development, motivation, diversity and need. - ED.O.A2.1 Prior knowledge and misconceptions — e.g. the impetus misconception in force and motion (physics education research). The cognitive mechanism is MS. - ED.O.A2.2 Development — age-related readiness, cited from MS. - ED.O.A2.3 Motivation and engagement. - ED.O.A2.4 Diversity and learning need — inclusion, special education, gifted learners. ### ED.O.A3 Teaching **SCQA.** Teaching arrangements cause learning, or fail

to. Which arrangements work, for whom? Key line: instruction, feedback, practice and retrieval, technology, culturally sustaining pedagogy. - ED.O.A3.1 Instruction — explicit instruction versus discovery; worked examples help novices (an expertise-reversal effect is a stated defeater for experts). - ED.O.A3.2 Feedback — effects vary widely by type; some feedback lowers performance (UNVERIFIED as a meta-analytic figure). - ED.O.A3.3 Practice and retrieval — spacing and retrieval practice improve long-term retention. The memory mechanism is MS. - ED.O.A3.4 Technology in teaching — effects depend on use, not presence. - ED.O.A3.5 Culturally sustaining

pedagogy — Kaupapa Māori education (kura kaupapa Māori) as an arrangement. The tradition-internal content is IK. ### ED.O.A4 Assessment **SCQA.** Learning is inferred from performance on instruments. What does a score mean? Key line: validity, reliability, formative assessment, high-stakes testing. - ED.O.A4.1 Validity — an argument that score interpretations are supported (W9 with W4). - ED.O.A4.2 Reliability — score consistency; the statistics are MA.O.A5 (psychometrics as bridge). - ED.O.A4.3 Formative assessment — assessment used to change teaching. - ED.O.A4.4 High-stakes testing and accountability — Campbell's law: the more a quantitative

indicator drives decisions, the more it is subject to corruption pressures (stated as a tendency). ### ED.O.A5 Institutions and systems **SCQA.** Teaching happens inside schools and systems with rules. What do institutions do to learning? Key line: schools, school systems, higher education, equity and access. - ED.O.A5.1 Schools — school effects, leadership, class size. - ED.O.A5.2 School systems — international comparisons (PISA, TIMSS) are W4 within their sampling designs. - ED.O.A5.3 Higher education — universities, credentials. - ED.O.A5.4 Equity and access — gaps by group. The returns to schooling are
EC; the law on schooling is LA.

## 2. Governing thought Design is exhausted by four faces of one pyramid: objects, methods, warrants and bridges. Its objects divide into five aspects of a designed arrangement: use and need, form, performance in use, place and settlement, and life of the built thing. ## 3. Key line Dimension: **the aspect of a designed arrangement for human use.** Order: from the need to the life of the result. 1. Use and need 2. Form 3. Performance in use 4. Place and settlement 5. Life of the built thing ## 4.

Face O — Objects ### DE.O.A1 Use and need **SCQA.** Design starts from people's use. What need does the arrangement serve? Key line: users and activities, the brief, accessibility. - DE.O.A1.1 Users and activities — who will use it and how. Human factors cite MS. - DE.O.A1.2 The brief — the stated programme of needs (W12 once agreed). - DE.O.A1.3 Accessibility and universal design — designing for the widest range of users. ### DE.O.A2 Form **SCQA.** Needs are answered by spatial and visual arrangements. What form, and why? Key line:

spatial organisation, typology, visual and material language. - DE.O.A2.1 Spatial organisation — plan, section, circulation. - DE.O.A2.2 Typology — building and product types. - DE.O.A2.3 Visual and material language — composition, colour, materials. An aesthetic verdict with a stated criterion is AR.O.A5. ### DE.O.A3 Performance in use **SCQA.** A design is judged by how it works for its users. Key line: comfort and environment, wayfinding and usability, safety in use, post-occupancy evaluation. - DE.O.A3.1 Comfort and indoor environment — thermal, acoustic, daylight. The physics is PH; structural adequacy is EN.

- DE.O.A3.2 Wayfinding and usability. - DE.O.A3.3 Safety in use — building codes are W12; their legal force is LA. - DE.O.A3.4 Post-occupancy evaluation — measured performance after use begins (W4). ### DE.O.A4 Place and settlement **SCQA.** Designs sit in places and form settlements. Key line: site, urban form, landscape, planning. - DE.O.A4.1 Site — the physical site claim uses EA. - DE.O.A4.2 Urban form — density, street networks, mixed use. - DE.O.A4.3 Landscape architecture. - DE.O.A4.4 Planning — zoning and land use. The legal instrument is LA; the political

decision is PO. ### DE.O.A5 Life of the built thing **SCQA.** Built things age, are kept, adapted and removed. Key line: maintenance and adaptation, sustainability, heritage conservation. - DE.O.A5.1 Maintenance and adaptive reuse. - DE.O.A5.2 Sustainability — embodied and operational carbon. The environmental impact claim is EV. - DE.O.A5.3 Conservation of built heritage — the heritage meaning is HI.O.A5.3.

## 2. Governing thought Agriculture is exhausted by four faces of one pyramid: objects, methods, warrants and bridges. Its objects divide into five stages of production: breeding, cultivation and husbandry, crop and animal health, food, and farming systems. ## 3. Key line Dimension: **the stage of the production system.** Order: from the organism to the whole system. 1. Breeding 2. Cultivation and husbandry 3. Crop and animal health 4. Food 5. Farming systems ## 4. Face O — Objects ### AG.O.A1 Breeding **SCQA.** Production starts with chosen organisms. How are

they improved? Key line: selection, genetic improvement, genetic resources. - AG.O.A1.1 Selection — the breeder's equation R = h²S predicts response to selection, assuming additive inheritance and a stable environment. The genetics is BI. - AG.O.A1.2 Genetic improvement — hybrids, marker-assisted selection, gene editing. Regulation is LA. - AG.O.A1.3 Genetic resources — seed banks, landraces. ### AG.O.A2 Cultivation and husbandry **SCQA.** Organisms are grown and kept under managed conditions. What management gives what result? Key line: soils and nutrients, water, crop management, animal husbandry, aquaculture and forestry. - AG.O.A2.1 Soils

and nutrients — fertiliser response. Liebig's law of the minimum holds as a first approximation, when one nutrient limits growth. The soil's state is EA. - AG.O.A2.2 Water and irrigation. - AG.O.A2.3 Crop management — rotation, tillage, sowing. A yield claim must state season, site and population. - AG.O.A2.4 Animal husbandry — pastoral and housed systems, nutrition, welfare. NZ pastoral dairying is a substrate. - AG.O.A2.5 Aquaculture, fisheries and forestry production. ### AG.O.A3 Crop and animal health **SCQA.** Producing organisms fall ill and are attacked. How is their health kept?

Key line: plant protection, veterinary medicine, biosecurity, zoonoses. - AG.O.A3.1 Plant protection — pests, weeds, pathogens; integrated pest management. - AG.O.A3.2 Veterinary medicine — diagnosis and treatment of animal disorders. - AG.O.A3.3 Biosecurity — border and incursion management (e.g. Mycoplasma bovis in NZ from 2017, UNVERIFIED date). - AG.O.A3.4 Zoonoses — the animal side is AG; human disease is MD (One Health is a bridge). ### AG.O.A4 Food **SCQA.** Produce becomes food. What makes food safe, nutritious and stable? Key line: composition and nutrition, processing, safety, standards. - AG.O.A4.1 Composition

and nutrition — the molecule is CH; human nutritional need is MD. - AG.O.A4.2 Processing and preservation — fermentation, pasteurisation, drying. - AG.O.A4.3 Food safety — HACCP as a control system (W11); pathogen limits. - AG.O.A4.4 Food standards — Codex Alimentarius; FSANZ for Australia and NZ (W12; legal force LA). ### AG.O.A5 Farming systems **SCQA.** Farms are systems of land, organisms, labour and markets. Key line: system productivity, farm management, environmental effect. - AG.O.A5.1 System productivity — total factor productivity of farms (measurement here; economics EC). - AG.O.A5.2 Farm management
— decisions under weather and price risk. - AG.O.A5.3 Environmental effect of farming — nitrate leaching, methane. The impact claim is EV; AG owns the practice that changes it.

## 2. Governing thought Environmental science is exhausted by four faces of one pyramid: objects, methods, warrants and bridges. Its objects divide into five links of a coupled system: pressures, states, impacts, responses, and limits. ## 3. Key line Dimension: **the link in the human–environment causal chain.** Order: causal. 1. Pressures 2. States 3. Impacts 4. Responses 5. Limits ## 4. Face O — Objects ### EV.O.A1 Pressures **SCQA.** Human activity loads the environment. What load, from what activity? Key line: emissions, land and sea use change, extraction, introduced species.

- EV.O.A1.1 Emissions — greenhouse gases, pollutants. Inventories follow IPCC guidelines (W12 for method). - EV.O.A1.2 Land and sea use change — clearance, drainage, urbanisation. - EV.O.A1.3 Extraction — water, fish, minerals. - EV.O.A1.4 Introduced species — pests and invasives (e.g. possums and mustelids in NZ). ### EV.O.A2 States **SCQA.** Pressures change the state of air, water, soil and biota. What is the measured state? Key line: air, freshwater, marine, soil, biodiversity. - EV.O.A2.1 Air quality — the measurement uses CH and EA. - EV.O.A2.2 Freshwater quality — nitrate, E.

coli, sediment. - EV.O.A2.3 Marine environment — acidification, warming. - EV.O.A2.4 Soil state — contamination, erosion. - EV.O.A2.5 Biodiversity status — threat classifications (IUCN Red List criteria, W12). ### EV.O.A3 Impacts **SCQA.** A changed state harms ecosystems and people. What harm, attributed how? Key line: ecosystem harm, human health impact, attribution, ecosystem services. - EV.O.A3.1 Ecosystem harm — loss of function and species. - EV.O.A3.2 Human health impact — the exposure–response is MD. - EV.O.A3.3 Attribution — the share of an observed change caused by a stated pressure (e.g. event

attribution in climate science). The physical model is EA. - EV.O.A3.4 Ecosystem services — benefits people receive; valuation is EC. ### EV.O.A4 Responses **SCQA.** Societies respond. Which responses change pressures or states? Key line: restoration, conservation, regulation, monitoring of outcomes. - EV.O.A4.1 Restoration — measured recovery after intervention. - EV.O.A4.2 Conservation — protected areas, predator control (Predator Free 2050 is a stated goal, UNVERIFIED name and date). - EV.O.A4.3 Regulation and instruments — the policy is PO, the price instrument EC, the duty LA. EV owns the measured environmental effect.

- EV.O.A4.4 Kaitiakitanga in practice — guardianship as a response; its tradition-internal meaning is IK. ### EV.O.A5 Limits **SCQA.** Some states should not be crossed. Where are the limits? Key line: thresholds and tipping points, standards, carrying capacity and boundaries. - EV.O.A5.1 Thresholds and tipping points — a regime shift occurs past a critical value, assuming bistable dynamics (theory MA.O.A4). - EV.O.A5.2 Standards and bottom lines — legal or agreed limits (W12; force LA). - EV.O.A5.3 Carrying capacity and planetary boundaries — the planetary boundaries framework (Rockström et al., 2009)
is a proposed set, CONTESTED in its numbers.

## 2. Governing thought Information science is exhausted by four faces of one pyramid: objects, methods, warrants and bridges. Its objects divide into five stages of a record's life: items, description, arrangement, retrieval, and preservation. ## 3. Key line Dimension: **the stage in the life of a record.** Order: from creation to keeping. 1. Items 2. Description 3. Arrangement 4. Retrieval 5. Preservation ## 4. Face O — Objects ### IS.O.A1 Items **SCQA.** A record must first be identified as a unit. What is the item? Key line: works and

manifestations, records and evidence, data sets, identifiers. - IS.O.A1.1 Works and manifestations — FRBR and its successor LRM distinguish work, expression, manifestation and item. - IS.O.A1.2 Records as evidence — an archival record is evidence of an activity. Its source criticism for history is HI. - IS.O.A1.3 Data sets — research data as items. - IS.O.A1.4 Persistent identifiers — DOI, ORCID, ISBN (W12). ### IS.O.A2 Description **SCQA.** Items are found by their descriptions. How are they described? Key line: metadata standards, cataloguing rules, subject indexing, linked data. - IS.O.A2.1 Metadata

standards — Dublin Core, MARC (W12). - IS.O.A2.2 Cataloguing rules — RDA. - IS.O.A2.3 Subject indexing — controlled vocabularies and thesauri (MeSH, LCSH). - IS.O.A2.4 Linked data — SKOS and RDF. The logic is MA.O.A1; the vocabulary is IS. ### IS.O.A3 Arrangement **SCQA.** Descriptions are organised into schemes. How is knowledge arranged? Key line: classification schemes, faceted classification, archival arrangement, ontologies. - IS.O.A3.1 Classification schemes — LCC, DDC, UDC, MSC. A scheme is W12; whether it is MECE is testable (W9 with W4). - IS.O.A3.2 Faceted classification — Ranganathan's Colon

Classification (PMEST facets). - IS.O.A3.3 Archival arrangement — respect des fonds and original order. - IS.O.A3.4 Ontologies — BFO and DOLCE. Their philosophical commitments are PL. - IS.O.A3.5 This taxonomy — the Pyramids of Knowledge as a classification of claims. Its reliability is tested by the placement protocol. ### IS.O.A4 Retrieval **SCQA.** Arranged records must be found. How well can they be found? Key line: retrieval effectiveness, relevance, bibliometrics, information behaviour. - IS.O.A4.1 Retrieval effectiveness — precision and recall. The algorithm's cost is CS. - IS.O.A4.2 Relevance — topical and

user relevance; judged by assessors (W4). - IS.O.A4.3 Bibliometrics — Lotka's law (author productivity) and Bradford's law (scattering) are empirical regularities within stated literatures. - IS.O.A4.4 Information behaviour — how people seek information. The cognitive mechanism is MS. ### IS.O.A5 Preservation **SCQA.** Records decay and formats die. How are they kept usable? Key line: physical conservation, digital preservation, access and rights, Indigenous data governance. - IS.O.A5.1 Physical conservation — the chemistry of paper and media is CH. - IS.O.A5.2 Digital preservation — the OAIS reference model (ISO 14721, W12). -

IS.O.A5.3 Access and rights — open access; copyright is LA. - IS.O.A5.4 Indigenous data governance — the CARE principles; Māori data sovereignty (Te Mana Raraunga). Tradition-internal authority over the data is IK.

## 2. Governing thought Indigenous knowledge is exhausted by four faces of one pyramid: objects, methods, warrants and bridges. Its objects divide into five aspects of a knowledge system: ordering principles, relations to land and waters, governance and custom, transmission, and research and data. ## 3. Key line Dimension: **the aspect of a knowledge system the claim is about.** Order: from the system's principles to its relation with outside research. 1. Ordering principles 2. Relations to land and waters 3. Governance and custom 4. Transmission 5. Research and data A

people (iwi, hapū, nation) is a substrate, not a cell. A ·M sentence names its iwi or hapū, because authority is local. ## 4. Face O — Objects ### IK.O.A1 Ordering principles **SCQA.** A knowledge system orders the world by its own principles. What are they, as held? Key line: whakapapa as an ordering principle, categories of status, cyclical time. - IK.O.A1.1 Whakapapa as ordering — genealogy as the principle that relates people, atua and the natural world. Whakapapa as human descent is HI; whakapapa of atua is RE. -

IK.O.A1.2 Categories of status — tapu and noa as ordering categories outside rite (in rite, RE.O.A1.2). - IK.O.A1.3 Cyclical and ancestral time — "ka mua, ka muri" (walking backwards into the future) as a stated orientation (·S W8; ·M W13). ### IK.O.A2 Relations to land and waters **SCQA.** Knowledge systems hold relations to particular places. What is claimed about that relation? Key line: kaitiakitanga, maramataka, place knowledge. - IK.O.A2.1 Kaitiakitanga — guardianship as obligation. Its measured environmental effect is EV.O.A4.4. - IK.O.A2.2 Maramataka — the lunar calendar as a system

for timing activity. An ecological observation it records (a fish run) is BI or EA under W4; the system itself is IK. - IK.O.A2.3 Place knowledge — names, boundaries and histories of places, held by mana whenua. The landform is EA; the dated event is HI. ### IK.O.A3 Governance and custom **SCQA.** Communities govern themselves by custom and authority. Key line: tikanga as custom, rangatiratanga, marae kawa, customary institutions. - IK.O.A3.1 Tikanga as custom — correct practice in social life. In rite before atua it is RE.O.A3.1. As recognised by

a state court it is LA.O.A1.3. - IK.O.A3.2 Rangatiratanga — authority and self-determination as held. Its Treaty and legal dimension is LA.O.A4.4; its political dimension is PO. - IK.O.A3.3 Marae kawa — the protocols of a particular marae (local, ·M). - IK.O.A3.4 Customary institutions — rūnanga, hui as decision forums. ### IK.O.A4 Transmission **SCQA.** Knowledge lives only if transmitted. How is it passed on, and who may hold it? Key line: institutions of learning, oral and performed transmission, restricted knowledge. - IK.O.A4.1 Institutions of learning — whare wānanga, past and

present. Modern wānanga as tertiary institutions are ED. - IK.O.A4.2 Oral and performed transmission — kōrero tuku iho, mōteatea, haka. Their poetics are AR; their language is LN. - IK.O.A4.3 Restricted knowledge — knowledge held by designated people and not for open classification. The pyramid records that restriction exists, never the content. ### IK.O.A5 Research and data **SCQA.** Outside research has often taken Indigenous knowledge without consent. What rules govern research and data? Key line: Kaupapa Māori research, data sovereignty, consent and benefit. - IK.O.A5.1 Kaupapa Māori research — research

by, with and for Māori, under Māori control (Smith, *Decolonizing Methodologies*, 1999). - IK.O.A5.2 Data sovereignty — Te Mana Raraunga principles; the CARE principles. The records framework is IS.O.A5.4. - IK.O.A5.3 Consent and benefit — Wai 262 (*Ko Aotearoa Tēnei*, 2011) on flora, fauna and mātauranga (UNVERIFIED date). Legal effect is LA.
